## Snake survey hotspots at Elephants by the Lake (EBTL), Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu

### Site context

EBTL is a ~68-acre forest restoration project on undulating, formerly denuded land in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats, near Chinnathamandrapalli village, Veppanapalli town, Krishnagiri district (~12.5N, 78.2E). The landscape is dry deciduous/thorn scrub forest at ~300-600m elevation, with surrounding granite hills, an old elephant waterhole, farmland, and active permaculture restoration. EBTL's own research programme explicitly targets herpetofauna as ecosystem health indicators [1].

The best analog datasets come from:

- **Ganesh et al. (2018)** -- 1000-hour survey of the Southern Eastern Ghats including the Krishnagiri-area ranges, recording 37 snake species [2]
- **Karthik (2016)** -- 120-hour microhabitat survey at Gingee Hills (same Eastern Ghats dry deciduous/thorn scrub biome, ~150 km east), recording 21 snake species with explicit microhabitat assignments [3]
- **Ganesh et al. (2021)** -- Central Eastern Ghats survey, 42 snake species, describing open rocky scrub vs. tree-covered woodland as the two dominant habitat types and noting that snakes partition between them [4]
- **Surendran & Livingstone (2023)** -- radio-tracking of *Python molurus* in Moyar River Valley (same forest types), showing 30% of sightings in green bushes, 30% in dry bushes, 12% in rocky crevices, 6% on open ground, and only 1% near water (but females were significantly more water-associated) [5]
- **Thorpe & Ganesh (2021)** -- *Cnemaspis krishnagiriensis* described from granite boulder habitat at Krishnagiri Fort, confirming the local landscape has classic rupicolous (rock-dwelling) herpetofauna niches [6]

### Ranked survey hotspots (most to least productive)

**1. Rocky outcrops, boulder piles, and stone walls (highest priority)**

This is your single best microhabitat. In the Eastern Ghats dry zone, granite boulders, loose rock piles, and old stone walls harbour the most specialist snake species and the highest encounter rates per unit effort. Species expected:
- *Echis carinatus* (saw-scaled viper) -- under flat rocks on rocky substrate, the dominant venomous snake of this habitat [7]
- *Lycodon aulicus* / *L. flavicollis* -- under rocks at night
- *Boiga* spp. (cat snakes) -- rock-face crevices and adjacent scrub
- Blind snakes (*Indotyphlops braminus*, *Gerrhopilus* spp.) -- under embedded rocks in moist soil
- *Uropeltis* shieldtails -- fossorial under boulders on hillslopes

**Survey method:** Turn rocks (replace after), check crevices with a torch at night. Best Nov-Feb (post-monsoon, cool season, when snakes shelter under rocks for thermoregulation). Focus on the granite hillslopes surrounding the EBTL valley and any stone walls/bund walls within the farmland zone.

**2. Forest floor with deep leaf litter and fallen logs (high priority)**

The largest guild of reptiles in comparable Southern Indian communities is the "forest floor-dwelling" guild (25 of 47 species in the Agasthyamalai study [8]). At EBTL, as restoration matures and leaf litter accumulates, this zone will grow in importance.

Species expected:
- *Coelognathus helena* (trinket snake) -- leaf litter and low scrub
- *Ptyas mucosa* (rat snake) -- generalist, but forages in litter
- *Sibynophis subpunctatus* -- in insect holes and under dense leaf litter [9]
- *Calliophis melanurus* (slender coral snake) -- loose soil under litter
- Skink-hunting snakes (*Oligodon* spp.) -- under logs

**Survey method:** Visual Encounter Survey (VES) along transects through the restored native forest patches, flipping logs and raking litter. Best after rains (June-December), when litter is moist and arthropod prey is active.

**3. Waterhole edges and seasonal stream/nala margins (moderate-high priority)**

EBTL has a named waterhole (the "lake" in its name) and likely seasonal nalas draining the surrounding hills. Water edges concentrate prey (frogs, fish, crabs) and provide humidity refugia.

Species expected:
- *Atretium schistosum* (olive keelback) -- semi-aquatic, recorded in Gingee Hills [3]
- *Xenochrophis piscator* (checkered keelback) -- the most commonly encountered water snake in this landscape
- *Amphiesma stolatum* (buff-striped keelback) -- marshy edges
- *Python molurus* -- tracked females show significant water-body association [5]
- *Naja naja* (spectacled cobra) -- generalist but frequently found near water, especially where frogs breed

**Survey method:** Night walks along water margins with headlamps, especially during and just after monsoon (July-November). Check under stones and debris within 5m of the waterline.

**4. Farmland-forest edge and bund walls (moderate priority)**

EBTL actively manages paddy, pulses, and millet fields adjacent to the restoration area. The ecotone between cultivated land and scrub forest is a synanthropic snake hotspot.

Species expected:
- *Naja naja* -- strongly associated with rodent-rich farm edges
- *Daboia russelii* (Russell's viper) -- if present in the area, found in scrub-farm margins
- *Ptyas mucosa* -- follows rodent concentrations
- *Eryx* spp. (sand boas) -- in loose, tilled soil
- *Lycodon aulicus* (common wolf snake) -- stone bunds and building foundations

**Survey method:** Night road cruising (if paths exist between fields and forest) and checking irrigation channels, compost heaps, and stone bunds. Year-round, but peak encounters in monsoon.

**5. Thorn scrub and open, dry ground (lower priority, but important for specialists)**

The drier open scrub zones at low elevation (<300m) are lower in overall density but host specialist dry-zone species.

Species expected:
- *Psammophis condanarus* / *P. longifrons* (sand snakes) -- fast-moving, diurnal, in open scrub [4]
- *Argyrogena fasciolata* (banded racer) -- open scrub and paths
- *Echis carinatus* -- also uses open rocky scrub at night

**Survey method:** Diurnal visual searches along trails during warm months (March-May). Night driving/walking in dry season.

### Timing summary

| Season | Best microhabitats | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Monsoon (Jun-Dec) | Water edges, leaf litter, farmland edges | Prey activity peaks, frogs breed, snakes are surface-active |
| Post-monsoon cool (Nov-Feb) | Rocky outcrops, boulder piles | Snakes thermoregulate under rocks; turning rocks is most productive |
| Hot dry (Mar-May) | Waterhole edges, open scrub (diurnal for sand snakes) | Snakes concentrate near remaining water; dry-zone specialists active |

### Bottom line

**Rocky ground is your single best bet** -- it concentrates both diversity and encounter rate in this landscape, and Krishnagiri specifically has documented rupicolous herpetofauna endemics. **Water margins are second**, especially during and after monsoon. Leaf litter zones will become increasingly important as EBTL's restoration matures and canopy cover builds.

---

## Snake survey hotspots at Elephants by the Lake (EBTL), Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu

### Site context

EBTL is a ~68-acre forest restoration project on undulating, formerly denuded land in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats, near Chinnathamandrapalli village, Veppanapalli town, Krishnagiri district (~12.5N, 78.2E). The landscape is dry deciduous/thorn scrub forest at ~300-600m elevation, with surrounding granite hills, an old elephant waterhole, farmland, and active permaculture restoration. EBTL's own research programme explicitly targets herpetofauna as ecosystem health indicators [1].

The best analog datasets come from:

- **Ganesh et al. (2018)** -- 1000-hour survey of the Southern Eastern Ghats including the Krishnagiri-area ranges, recording 37 snake species [2]
- **Karthik (2016)** -- 120-hour microhabitat survey at Gingee Hills (same Eastern Ghats dry deciduous/thorn scrub biome, ~150 km east), recording 21 snake species with explicit microhabitat assignments [3]
- **Ganesh et al. (2021)** -- Central Eastern Ghats survey, 42 snake species, describing open rocky scrub vs. tree-covered woodland as the two dominant habitat types and noting that snakes partition between them [4]
- **Surendran & Livingstone (2023)** -- radio-tracking of *Python molurus* in Moyar River Valley (same forest types), showing 30% of sightings in green bushes, 30% in dry bushes, 12% in rocky crevices, 6% on open ground, and only 1% near water (but females were significantly more water-associated) [5]
- **Thorpe & Ganesh (2021)** -- *Cnemaspis krishnagiriensis* described from granite boulder habitat at Krishnagiri Fort, confirming the local landscape has classic rupicolous (rock-dwelling) herpetofauna niches [6]

### Ranked survey hotspots (most to least productive)

**1. Rocky outcrops, boulder piles, and stone walls (highest priority)**

This is your single best microhabitat. In the Eastern Ghats dry zone, granite boulders, loose rock piles, and old stone walls harbour the most specialist snake species and the highest encounter rates per unit effort. Species expected:
- *Echis carinatus* (saw-scaled viper) -- under flat rocks on rocky substrate, the dominant venomous snake of this habitat [7]
- *Lycodon aulicus* / *L. flavicollis* -- under rocks at night
- *Boiga* spp. (cat snakes) -- rock-face crevices and adjacent scrub
- Blind snakes (*Indotyphlops braminus*, *Gerrhopilus* spp.) -- under embedded rocks in moist soil
- *Uropeltis* shieldtails -- fossorial under boulders on hillslopes

**Survey method:** Turn rocks (replace after), check crevices with a torch at night. Best Nov-Feb (post-monsoon, cool season, when snakes shelter under rocks for thermoregulation). Focus on the granite hillslopes surrounding the EBTL valley and any stone walls/bund walls within the farmland zone.

**2. Forest floor with deep leaf litter and fallen logs (high priority)**

The largest guild of reptiles in comparable Southern Indian communities is the "forest floor-dwelling" guild (25 of 47 species in the Agasthyamalai study [8]). At EBTL, as restoration matures and leaf litter accumulates, this zone will grow in importance.

Species expected:
- *Coelognathus helena* (trinket snake) -- leaf litter and low scrub
- *Ptyas mucosa* (rat snake) -- generalist, but forages in litter
- *Sibynophis subpunctatus* -- in insect holes and under dense leaf litter [9]
- *Calliophis melanurus* (slender coral snake) -- loose soil under litter
- Skink-hunting snakes (*Oligodon* spp.) -- under logs

**Survey method:** Visual Encounter Survey (VES) along transects through the restored native forest patches, flipping logs and raking litter. Best after rains (June-December), when litter is moist and arthropod prey is active.

**3. Waterhole edges and seasonal stream/nala margins (moderate-high priority)**

EBTL has a named waterhole (the "lake" in its name) and likely seasonal nalas draining the surrounding hills. Water edges concentrate prey (frogs, fish, crabs) and provide humidity refugia.

Species expected:
- *Atretium schistosum* (olive keelback) -- semi-aquatic, recorded in Gingee Hills [3]
- *Xenochrophis piscator* (checkered keelback) -- the most commonly encountered water snake in this landscape
- *Amphiesma stolatum* (buff-striped keelback) -- marshy edges
- *Python molurus* -- tracked females show significant water-body association [5]
- *Naja naja* (spectacled cobra) -- generalist but frequently found near water, especially where frogs breed

**Survey method:** Night walks along water margins with headlamps, especially during and just after monsoon (July-November). Check under stones and debris within 5m of the waterline.

**4. Farmland-forest edge and bund walls (moderate priority)**

EBTL actively manages paddy, pulses, and millet fields adjacent to the restoration area. The ecotone between cultivated land and scrub forest is a synanthropic snake hotspot.

Species expected:
- *Naja naja* -- strongly associated with rodent-rich farm edges
- *Daboia russelii* (Russell's viper) -- if present in the area, found in scrub-farm margins
- *Ptyas mucosa* -- follows rodent concentrations
- *Eryx* spp. (sand boas) -- in loose, tilled soil
- *Lycodon aulicus* (common wolf snake) -- stone bunds and building foundations

**Survey method:** Night road cruising (if paths exist between fields and forest) and checking irrigation channels, compost heaps, and stone bunds. Year-round, but peak encounters in monsoon.

**5. Thorn scrub and open, dry ground (lower priority, but important for specialists)**

The drier open scrub zones at low elevation (<300m) are lower in overall density but host specialist dry-zone species.

Species expected:
- *Psammophis condanarus* / *P. longifrons* (sand snakes) -- fast-moving, diurnal, in open scrub [4]
- *Argyrogena fasciolata* (banded racer) -- open scrub and paths
- *Echis carinatus* -- also uses open rocky scrub at night

**Survey method:** Diurnal visual searches along trails during warm months (March-May). Night driving/walking in dry season.

### Timing summary

| Season | Best microhabitats | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Monsoon (Jun-Dec) | Water edges, leaf litter, farmland edges | Prey activity peaks, frogs breed, snakes are surface-active |
| Post-monsoon cool (Nov-Feb) | Rocky outcrops, boulder piles | Snakes thermoregulate under rocks; turning rocks is most productive |
| Hot dry (Mar-May) | Waterhole edges, open scrub (diurnal for sand snakes) | Snakes concentrate near remaining water; dry-zone specialists active |

### Bottom line

**Rocky ground is your single best bet** -- it concentrates both diversity and encounter rate in this landscape, and Krishnagiri specifically has documented rupicolous herpetofauna endemics. **Water margins are second**, especially during and after monsoon. Leaf litter zones will become increasingly important as EBTL's restoration matures and canopy cover builds.

---

## Snake survey hotspots at Elephants by the Lake (EBTL), Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu

### Site context

EBTL is a ~68-acre forest restoration project on undulating, formerly denuded land in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats, near Chinnathamandrapalli village, Veppanapalli town, Krishnagiri district (~12.5N, 78.2E). The landscape is dry deciduous/thorn scrub forest at ~300-600m elevation, with surrounding granite hills, an old elephant waterhole, farmland, and active permaculture restoration. EBTL's own research programme explicitly targets herpetofauna as ecosystem health indicators [1].

The best analog datasets come from:

- **Ganesh et al. (2018)** -- 1000-hour survey of the Southern Eastern Ghats including the Krishnagiri-area ranges, recording 37 snake species [2]
- **Karthik (2016)** -- 120-hour microhabitat survey at Gingee Hills (same Eastern Ghats dry deciduous/thorn scrub biome, ~150 km east), recording 21 snake species with explicit microhabitat assignments [3]
- **Ganesh et al. (2021)** -- Central Eastern Ghats survey, 42 snake species, describing open rocky scrub vs. tree-covered woodland as the two dominant habitat types and noting that snakes partition between them [4]
- **Surendran & Livingstone (2023)** -- radio-tracking of *Python molurus* in Moyar River Valley (same forest types), showing 30% of sightings in green bushes, 30% in dry bushes, 12% in rocky crevices, 6% on open ground, and only 1% near water (but females were significantly more water-associated) [5]

**1. Rocky outcrops, boulder piles, and stone walls (highest priority)**

This is your single best microhabitat. In the Eastern Ghats dry zone, granite boulders, loose rock piles, and old stone walls harbour the most specialist snake species and the highest encounter rates per unit effort. Species expected:
- *Echis carinatus* (saw-scaled viper) -- under flat rocks on rocky substrate, the dominant venomous snake of this habitat [7]
- *Lycodon aulicus* / *L. flavicollis* -- under rocks at night
- *Boiga* spp. (cat snakes) -- rock-face crevices and adjacent scrub
- Blind snakes (*Indotyphlops braminus*, *Gerrhopilus* spp.) -- under embedded rocks in moist soil
- *Uropeltis* shieldtails -- fossorial under boulders on hillslopes

**2. Forest floor with deep leaf litter and fallen logs (high priority)**

The largest guild of reptiles in comparable Southern Indian communities is the "forest floor-dwelling" guild (25 of 47 species in the Agasthyamalai study [8]). At EBTL, as restoration matures and leaf litter accumulates, this zone will grow in importance.

- *Coelognathus helena* (trinket snake) -- leaf litter and low scrub
- *Ptyas mucosa* (rat snake) -- generalist, but forages in litter

- *Python molurus* -- tracked females show significant water-body association [5]
- *Naja naja* (spectacled cobra) -- generalist but frequently found near water, especially where frogs breed

**Survey method:** Night walks along water margins with headlamps, especially during and just after monsoon (July-November). Check under stones and debris within 5m of the waterline.

EBTL actively manages paddy, pulses, and millet fields adjacent to the restoration area. The ecotone between cultivated land and scrub forest is a synanthropic snake hotspot.

Species expected:
- *Naja naja* -- strongly associated with rodent-rich farm edges
- *Daboia russelii* (Russell's viper) -- if present in the area, found in scrub-farm margins
- *Ptyas mucosa* -- follows rodent concentrations
- *Eryx* spp. (sand boas) -- in loose, tilled soil
- *Lycodon aulicus* (common wolf snake) -- stone bunds and building foundations

**Survey method:** Night road cruising (if paths exist between fields and forest) and checking irrigation channels, compost heaps, and stone bunds. Year-round, but peak encounters in monsoon.

- *Psammophis condanarus* / *P. longifrons* (sand snakes) -- fast-moving, diurnal, in open scrub [4]
- *Argyrogena fasciolata* (banded racer) -- open scrub and paths

**Survey method:** Diurnal visual searches along trails during warm months (March-May). Night driving/walking in dry season.

| Monsoon (Jun-Dec) | Water edges, leaf litter, farmland edges | Prey activity peaks, frogs breed, snakes are surface-active |

### Bottom line

**Rocky ground is your single best bet** -- it concentrates both diversity and encounter rate in this landscape, and Krishnagiri specifically has documented rupicolous herpetofauna endemics. **Water margins are second**, especially during and after monsoon.
